source.title: Regression as Classification: Influence of Task Formulation on Neural Network Features
source.authors: Lawrence Stewart; F. Bach; Quentin Berthet; Jean-Philippe Vert

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own synthetic regression experiments, but they concern validation RMSE and learned feature supports for square-loss regression versus binned cross-entropy classification. They do not test the training-classification-error outcomes named in V1–V6. The paper cites prior work on local minima and initialization but does not test those cited results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for its own task-formulation experiments. It also mentions results from prior work, including Safran and Shamir (2018); those cited results are not rows. Gradient trajectories and feature-support plots are discussed, but they do not measure a claim version’s named outcome.
record.test_reason: The study compares square-loss regression with binned classification on synthetic teacher-generated data. It does not test any listed version: in particular, it does not vary teacher–student widths or measure how one or two extra neurons change spurious-minimum frequency as V2 specifies. Its training under-fitting result at 10,000 student neurons concerns a different condition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose differences in feature supports associated with simplified implicit-bias problems as one possible explanation for the binning advantage. Their synthetic experiments support that explanation empirically; they do not prove that these supports cause optimization failure. They explicitly report that deeper regression models avoided the observed under-fitting.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic one-dimensional regression and its binned classification reformulation; two-layer ReLU networks trained with gradient descent. The measurements are validation RMSE and feature supports, rather than training classification error on the listed benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: Task formulation and network depth: the reported two-layer regression under-fitting was not observed in the three-layer regression experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 30 initializations, two-layer square-loss regression had mean validation RMSE 0.0455 versus 0.0121 for binned classification. Every classification run outperformed the best regression run. The worst regression model missed small triangles in the training data despite having 10,000 hidden neurons versus the teacher's nine. A three-layer regression model avoided this under-fitting across ten initializations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On this synthetic teacher-generated task, substantial width alone did not prevent two-layer regression under-fitting; changing the loss formulation or adding a hidden layer improved fitting.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2023), Proceedings of the 26th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The empirical comparison is a synthetic task with one-dimensional inputs and 30 initializations for the two-layer comparison. The reported numeric metric is validation RMSE, not training error. The three-layer RMSE is presented only as a figure without numeric values. The paper states that the link between its proposed supports and optimization is only seen empirically.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Feature-support plots, gradient-angle plots, and the two-dimensional critical-line plots do not report an outcome named by any claim version.

untested.parts: Training classification error of convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted labels and model-size or training-recipe effects.
Spurious-minimum frequency as teacher and student widths grow together, and the effect of adding one or two student neurons within the specified widths.
Depth degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity-shortcut comparisons, and the specified deep tanh and Fixup settings.
Comparative effects of initialization on signal propagation, training speed, and trainable depth. Glorot initialization is used without an initialization comparison.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including the Fixup alternative.

record.verdict_notes: Section 7.3 contrasts the findings with Safran and Shamir, but does not reproduce or contradict V2's specified width experiment. The result cautions against extending that version into an unrestricted guarantee that overparameterization eliminates under-fitting.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and the effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization.
The student-versus-teacher width sweep and frequency of spurious minima; the Safran and Shamir result is cited, not tested.
Plain versus residual networks, batch normalization, ImageNet or CIFAR-10 training error, and the stated deep tanh and Fixup conditions.
Comparisons of initialization methods, their effects on training speed, and trainable depth.
Training above a stability limit, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence outcomes.
Batch normalization’s effect on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup’s corresponding normalization-free comparison.

rows.measure: Validation RMSE ×102 across 30 random initializations; population statistics
rows.note: This is validation RMSE, not training classification error. The paper says the worst-performing model was unable to fit smaller-scale triangles and converged to a local minimum of square loss.
rows.check: Table 1 statistics are correctly recorded but measure validation regression RMSE. The accompanying training under-fitting observation does not establish V2's width-dependent comparison.

rows.measure: Validation RMSE ×102 across 30 random initializations; population statistics
rows.note: The authors state every classification model attained lower validation error than the best-performing regression model. This measures validation regression error, not training classification error.
rows.check: Statistics are correctly recorded. Predictions are evaluated as real-valued regression outputs; this is neither training classification error under V1 nor a teacher–student width comparison under V2.

rows.subject: Regression model with two hidden layers
rows.size_stated: 1000 and 250 neurons in the two hidden layers; 252, 250 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Trained with square loss on the synthetic regression task for ten random weight initializations.
rows.note: The text explicitly says three-layer networks did not suffer the under-fitting observed for two-layer networks, but the plotted RMSE values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Appendix G reports a valid separate experiment, but its validation RMSE and removal of shallow-model under-fitting do not measure V3's degradation in deep plain convolutional networks or its shortcut comparison. Exact run values are unavailable in the supplied figure text.
